slides.title: Hidden prey are located through their electric fields
body: **Passive electroreception** is detection of electric fields produced outside the sensing animal, without probing the environment with its own discharge. Kalmijn tested feeding in small-spotted catsharks, _Scyliorhinus canicula_, and thornback rays, _Raja clavata_, using living plaice concealed beneath sand.

Catsharks made directed feeding turns when they passed within approximately 15 cm of buried prey. Because sand could still transmit odor and water movements, concealment alone did not isolate the sensory cue. Kalmijn therefore enclosed the plaice in electrically conductive agar and manipulated the information escaping from it.

Predators continued attacking the concealed living fish through agar, whereas pieces of whiting redirected searching toward the chamber’s water outlet. Electrical localization and odor-induced feeding motivation were experimentally separable. The result establishes short-range use of prey fields under these conditions, rather than unlimited detection through seawater.

slides.title: Conductive agar isolates the prey’s electrical cue
body: An **electric field** is a spatial voltage gradient that can drive current through a conductor. Kalmijn constructed a chamber from 3% agar in seawater, with thick sidewalls, a reinforced roof, and inlet and outlet tubes supplying the enclosed plaice with fresh seawater.

The chamber concealed the fish and attenuated mechanical disturbances while remaining conductive. A 1-Hz test current of 120 µA passed between electrodes 5 cm apart; field measurements with and without the chamber differed by no more than the reported 3% measurement limit.

Water carried potential odorants toward the outlet, yet attacks on living plaice were directed toward the agar-covered head region. The conductivity measurement was an essential control: a barrier cannot isolate an electrical cue unless its effect on that cue is tested independently. Agar screening reduced competing cues without denervating the predator.

slides.title: Electrical insulation abolishes directed attacks
body: Kalmijn covered the conductive agar chamber with polyethylene approximately 10 µm thick, then replaced the sand. The living plaice remained inside, and diffuse whiting odor still motivated the predators to search. The critical manipulation was electrical insulation around an otherwise similar concealed target.

Catsharks and rays passed close to the shielded fish without directed feeding responses. Removing the plastic restored attacks in control trials. The film had an area-specific resistance near 10¹² Ω·cm² and capacitance below 200 pF/cm², strongly attenuating direct-current and low-frequency fields.

The thin film added relatively little mechanical shielding compared with the reinforced agar roof. Reversible loss of localization therefore supports electrical guidance rather than an explanation based solely on sight, odor, or prey movement. This behavioral manipulation identifies a necessary available cue without measuring individual receptor-cell conductances.

slides.title: Artificial dipoles are sufficient to direct feeding
body: An **electric dipole** consists of a separated current source and sink. Kalmijn buried seawater-bridge outlets beneath sand and passed either a 1-Hz sinusoidal current or direct current of 4 µA between them, approximating the strength of a living plaice’s electrical signal.

After odor-induced arousal, catsharks and rays dug at the active outlets as though attacking prey. Identical buried outlets without current did not elicit these responses. In a competition test, a whiting piece 5 cm from the outlets supplied odor, but directed attacks favored the electrical source.

An artificial field was therefore sufficient for localization, while odor supplied a complementary motivational cue. Current-switching controls excluded the mere presence of electrodes as the target. The experiment does not establish that predators identify prey species from a dipole or that all natural bioelectric signals have the same waveform.

slides.title: A semi-natural arena measures shark orientation
body: Kajiura and Holland compared juvenile scalloped hammerheads, _Sphyrna lewini_, with sandbar sharks, _Carcharhinus plumbeus_, in an enclosed reef habitat. Both species consume bottom-associated fishes and crustaceans, permitting comparison of similar feeding tasks despite markedly different head shapes.

An overhead camera recorded sharks crossing an acrylic electrode plate in water less than 0.5 m deep. Each shark was isolated from companions during testing. Feeding odor encouraged searching, while electric current selected the active dipole independently of the other inactive targets.

Orientation was identified from a course change greater than 20° or a bite. Calibrated video allowed distance and trajectory measurements rather than relying only on observer descriptions. The semi-natural setting preserved swimming behavior, but odor stimulation and the plate constrained the encounter relative to unconstrained wild hunting.

slides.title: Controlled dipoles separate current from target position
body: The shark stimulus apparatus delivered a constant current of 6.0 µA through outlets separated by 1 cm. A battery-powered circuit and series ammeter controlled and monitored the stimulus. Four selectable dipoles allowed the experimenter to change the electrical target on the same plate.

Seawater-filled tubing separated the metal electrodes from the nearby swimming animal, reducing local chemical cues. Both species bit the active dipole and ignored inactive dipoles; repeated biting stopped when current was switched off. Target position and electrical activation were therefore independently manipulable.

Current in microamperes describes the source, whereas field strength in microvolts per centimeter describes the local stimulus encountered by the shark. These quantities are not interchangeable. Behavioral sensitivity requires the source geometry, seawater properties, distance, and encounter direction to be considered alongside the measured response.

slides.title: Hammerheads and sandbars have similar detection range
body: Kajiura and Holland measured distance from the dipole center when a shark initiated a directed turn. Hammerheads most often oriented within 5 cm, whereas sandbars most often oriented within 10 cm. The farthest responses were 30.6 cm and 31.6 cm, respectively.

The nearly identical maximum ranges did not support the prediction that the hammerhead’s expanded head necessarily produces a lower behavioral detection threshold. Both species searched the same apparatus with the same source current and dipole spacing, limiting differences caused by stimulus construction.

Maximum range and the most frequent response distance describe different aspects of performance. An occasional distant orientation does not imply that every encounter is detected there. The result applies to these juvenile species and motivated feeding conditions, rather than establishing identical sensitivity across all sharks or developmental stages.

slides.title: Encounter angle changes the detectable dipole field
body: A dipole’s field depends on direction as well as distance. Kajiura and Holland measured each shark’s approach angle relative to the line joining the two outlets. Orientations began farther away at smaller angles, where the relevant field component was stronger.

Both hammerheads and sandbars followed this relationship. Approaches nearer 90° required a closer encounter before an orientation began. Comparing orientation distance alone would therefore confound receptor sensitivity with the geometry of the sampled field; angle was needed to estimate the local electrical stimulus.

The two species encountered the source from many directions, so a distant response was not simply evidence of a preferred approach axis. The experiment relates swimming geometry to effective stimulation. It does not directly identify how downstream neurons combine the differing signals available at individual skin pores.

slides.title: Feeding responses occur at nanovolt gradients
body: Kajiura and Holland converted measured encounter geometry into estimated field intensity at orientation onset. Both shark species initiated approximately 70% of orientations below 0.1 µV/cm, and approximately 35–40% below 0.01 µV/cm. Their most sensitive responses were below 1 nV/cm.

The 6.0-µA, 1-cm dipole and calibrated video provided the common reference for these estimates. Inactive outlets and current-switching trials constrained explanations involving visible target marks or electrode-associated cues. The distributions broadly overlapped despite the conspicuous difference in head morphology.

A **behavioral threshold** is defined by an observable response criterion; it is not necessarily the threshold of one sensory cell. The lowest measured responses depend on source modeling and motivation. Strong sensitivity is established, while exact comparisons with isolated-cell membrane voltages require additional physiological measurements.

slides.title: A broad head changes the mechanics of orientation
body: The **cephalofoil** is the laterally expanded head of a hammerhead shark. Video sequences recorded the position of the head while a scalloped hammerhead turned toward the active dipole. The head edge nearest the source could remain nearly stationary as the trunk pivoted around it.

Sandbar sharks generally followed broader arcs. Because the maximum orientation distances were similar, the different trajectories could not be attributed simply to earlier detection by hammerheads. Head shape and trunk flexibility changed how a detected electrical target was brought toward the mouth.

The cephalofoil also samples a wider lateral search area, potentially increasing encounters with sources beneath the animal. Improved search coverage and turning mechanics are distinct from greater receptor sensitivity. The proposed hydrodynamic explanation fits the observed trajectories but was not tested by directly manipulating head shape.

slides.title: Body flexibility contributes to electrical prey capture
body: Kajiura and Holland quantified maximum trunk flexure during feeding turns. The mean measured angle was 85.9° in scalloped hammerheads and 113.3° in sandbars; the smaller angle represented a tighter bend. Body configuration was measured from video rather than inferred from the detection threshold.

The greater flexure of hammerheads was consistent with their rapid pivot orientations. Sandbars had broader trunks and typically used wider turning paths. The shared electrode apparatus distinguished these motor differences from differences in artificial-source spacing, current, or target availability.

Electroreception contributes to prey capture through a sensory-to-motor transformation, not merely by triggering a generic response. This study directly measured posture and trajectory, while the mechanical contribution of particular muscles or hydrodynamic forces remained an interpretation. Equal detection range can coexist with different interception performance.

slides.title: Skin pores connect to internal ampullary epithelia
body: The **ampullae of Lorenzini** are sensory organs in which skin pores connect through jelly-filled canals to an internal receptor epithelium. Bellono and colleagues examined the little skate, _Leucoraja erinacea_, using canal staining, organ dissection, and recordings from individual electrosensory cells.

Alcian Blue revealed the ventral canal network. Isolated ampullae retained short canal segments and attached afferent nerves, which carry sensory signals toward the brain; the published organ image has a 400-µm scale bar. Dissociated receptor cells were accessible to patch-clamp electrodes, with a 5-µm scale bar in the cellular preparation.

The pore samples external voltage. Receptor cells convert it into activity and **synaptic output**, transmission to sensory nerves through released chemicals called **neurotransmitters**. Canal anatomy explains access to an environmental signal but does not by itself identify the channel that amplifies it. Dissection allows mechanistic control while removing the intact animal’s spatial sampling.

slides.title: Ampullary jelly can conduct protons in vitro
body: Josberger and colleagues extracted ampullary jelly from sharks and skates and measured its electrical properties with controlled electrodes and humidity. A **proton** is a hydrogen ion, H⁺. Palladium-hydride contacts injected protons, whereas palladium contacts restricted their transfer into the sample.

At 75% relative humidity, a 1-V stimulus produced a proton-associated current peak near 250 nA, compared with approximately 10 nA for the ionic transient. Four-terminal measurements gave room-temperature proton conductivity near 2 mS/cm. Electrode comparisons separated charge-carrier behavior from a single undifferentiated current.

These are measurements of extracted material, not a direct recording of charge carriers traveling through a living canal during prey detection. The authors proposed that proton conduction may contribute to ampullary function. The intact organ’s physiological carrier balance and sensory advantage were not established by the material experiment.

slides.title: Jelly chemistry supports a conductive hydrogel
body: Josberger and colleagues characterized the jelly as a **hydrogel**, a hydrated polymer network. Prepared samples contained approximately 97% water. Drying reduced sample volume by about 80%, making hydration an essential experimental variable rather than a minor handling detail.

Chemical analyses identified sugars and sulfate-containing components consistent with keratan sulfate, a sulfated carbohydrate polymer. The original article combined compositional chromatography with infrared measurements. Sulfate groups could provide proton donors within a hydrated network, offering a possible material basis for measured proton conduction.

Chemical composition and electrical measurement support a conductive matrix, but they do not prove that keratan sulfate alone carries physiological sensory current. Species differences, hydration, electrode interfaces, and the intact canal remain relevant limitations. Material conduction must also be distinguished from membrane ion-channel amplification in receptor cells.

slides.title: An isolated ampulla separates epithelial and nerve signals
body: Clusin and Bennett isolated skate ampullae with canals and afferent nerves attached. Separate saline compartments allowed current and voltage measurements across the receptor epithelium. A salt bridge shunted the canal, keeping transampullary voltage close to its resting operating range.

Current delivered between compartments imposed small voltage stimuli without requiring a freely swimming animal. The investigators simultaneously monitored epithelial current and postsynaptic, or receiving-side, nerve responses. Removing or restoring the shunt changed the electrical load, allowing spontaneous activity to be separated from stimulus-induced output.

This preparation links an external electrical perturbation to receptor-organ current and a neural response. It preserves a tissue-level circuit but cannot independently voltage-clamp every receptor cell or distinguish all apical and basal conductances. Later single-cell recordings provide complementary channel-level evidence rather than replacing this organ-level result.

slides.title: Stimulus polarity changes synaptic drive to afferents
body: Clusin and Bennett applied small voltage steps to a shunted skate ampulla. body: A **primary afferent** is a sensory neuron carrying receptor output toward the central nervous system. slides.title: Near-threshold afferents have different response gains
body: **Gain** describes how strongly a neural response changes for a change in stimulus intensity. Tricas and New measured peak firing and resting firing while increasing a 1-Hz electric field. A high-gain example reached strong modulation near 0.5 µV/cm, while lower-gain units required larger gradients. The most sensitive afferents encoded peak gradients of approximately 20 nV/cm or less. slides.title: Skate BK passes less current per channel opening
body: Bellono and colleagues recorded individual BK channels in excised membrane patches from cells expressing skate or mouse subunits. **Single-channel conductance** measures current carried by one open channel for a specified driving force. slides.title: Reciprocal BK mutations identify pore adaptations
body: Bellono and colleagues substituted two skate BK residues with their mouse counterparts and performed the reciprocal substitutions in mouse BK. These residues lie near the intracellular pore, where local charge can influence potassium concentration. The comparison tested functional effects rather than sequence similarity alone.

slides.title: Channel modulation changes oscillations and behavior
body: Bellono and colleagues recorded spontaneous voltage oscillations in little-skate receptors and then manipulated channel activity. Nifedipine reduced calcium-dependent activity; BK blockade disrupted oscillations. The BK activator NS11021 reduced oscillation amplitude while increasing frequency, consistent with stronger repolarizing current.

Behaving skates were tested for preference toward a buried dipole during 30-minute trials. Vehicle and a calcium-channel drug ineffective against the measured current preserved target preference, whereas nifedipine and NS11021 reduced time near the active electrode. Subsequent startle tests checked for gross mobility impairment.

The paired physiological and behavioral perturbations connect channel activity to electrosensory performance. Whole-animal drug exposure is not restricted to the ampullae, so it does not prove that every behavioral effect originates exclusively in receptor cells. Startle controls limit a general motor explanation while leaving more specific sensory or systemic effects possible.

slides.title: Shark cells spike while skate cells oscillate
body: **Current clamp** measures membrane voltage while current is injected to change the cell’s operating point. The shared calcium mechanism and differing potassium feedback produce distinct cellular dynamics. Isolated-cell activity establishes a physiological difference, while its effect on natural stimulus discrimination requires synaptic and organismal tests.

body: Bellono and colleagues imposed voltage commands resembling recorded shark receptor spikes while measuring ionic currents. slides.title: Ribbon synapses organize receptor-to-nerve output
body: A **ribbon synapse** contains an intracellular structure that tethers vesicles near the release membrane. Bellono and colleagues used electron microscopy to examine shark and skate receptor synapses. Both species contained unusually long ribbons associated with vesicles and postsynaptic afferent endings.

The ribbons had similar shapes and tethered vesicles of comparable size and number. Shark receptors contained a larger readily releasable vesicle pool, whereas skate receptors contained more free cytoplasmic vesicles. The anatomical comparison accompanied measurements of faster release saturation in shark cells and more sustained responses in skate cells.

Pool organization offers a plausible explanation for release dynamics, but morphology alone cannot assign every vesicle’s eventual fate. The proposed refilling role of free vesicles draws on comparison with other ribbon synapses. Electron microscopy establishes synaptic architecture while capacitance and current recordings test its functional output.

slides.title: Androgen state alters afferent frequency tuning
body: Sisneros and Tricas implanted male Atlantic stingrays, _Dasyatis sabina_, with dihydrotestosterone, or DHT, an androgen hormone. Empty implants provided treatment controls. After 10–21 days, they recorded electrosensory afferents while varying the frequency of uniform electric-field stimulation.

Control afferents had peak sensitivity near 7–8 Hz, compared with approximately 5–6 Hz after DHT treatment. Responses from 0.5 to 4 Hz were approximately 2–4 dB higher in treated animals. Canal-group comparisons associated different tuning patterns with receptor anatomy and canal length.

The manipulation establishes hormonal modulation of peripheral sensory coding rather than a fixed species-wide frequency filter. The study did not identify the specific androgen-regulated channel or prove improved mating performance. Ecological tuning to conspecific ventilation is supported as an interpretation, while the recorded frequency shift is directly experimental.
